entries.title: Hungary to shut sole nuclear plant for first time on Sunday
entries.summary: Record-low water levels on the Danube forced the Paks plant offline, leaving Hungary facing a potential power crunch.
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

Record-low water levels on the Danube forced the Paks plant offline, leaving Hungary facing a potential power crunch.

Hungary will shut down the Paks nuclear power plant on Sunday for the first time in its 44-year history, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.

He made the announcement on social media late Saturday night, saying the decision was taken after a further drop in the Danube's water level.

The plant, located 120 kilometers (74.5 miles) south of the capital, Budapest, uses water from the Danube to cool its reactors. It provides more than 40% of Hungary's electricity generation.

Record-low Danube levels necessitated the shutdown

The Danube has fallen to record-low levels in some areas after months of below-average rainfall and successive heat waves since May.

Hungary's water authority projected that the Danube, which flows from Germany to the Black Sea, would fall further in the coming days.

It measured the Danube's water level in Budapest at 23 centimeters (9 inches) on Wednesday morning, well below the previous record low of 33 centimeters (13 inches) set in 2018.

As a result, output at the Paks nuclear power plant had already been cut earlier in the week and some reactors shut down.

"Due to a further decline in the Danube's water level, the second-to-last generating unit at the Paks nuclear power plant will be shut down at 1:30 a.m. (2330 GMT)," the prime minister said.

"As a result, the plant is now producing only 240 megawatts (of electricity), and tomorrow (on Sunday), for the first time in 44 years, it will be completely shut down," Magyar added.

Hungary's large power users asked to cut power

The surge in imported electricity prices could cost Hungary between 120 billion and 240 billion forints ($315 million to $630 million, €273 million to €546 million), Tisza Party Vice Chairman Mark Radnai said on Facebook.

Magyar warned the Paks plant could remain offline for weeks and said his government would seek voluntary power cuts from large users, in addition to the 240 megawatts already pledged, with penalties for noncompliance.

A decree would also allow grid operator MAVIR to mandate consumption cuts and temporarily disconnect large users if necessary.

"Households will be the last to face restrictions," Magyar said.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Homemade bomb goes off outside upscale Moscow restaurant state officials say
entries.summary: Russian authorities said the blast occurred outside a restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square when a woman allegedly carrying explosives was stopped by a security guard.
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

Russian authorities said the blast occurred outside a restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square when a woman allegedly carrying explosives was stopped by a security guard.

An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said.

Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying  "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard.

The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron.

What do we know about the explosion?

State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC).

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event.

Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation.

Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack.

Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: 13 killed in tourist plane crash in Peru
entries.summary: The plane was taking tourists to see the Nazca Lines, a group of geoglyphs etched into the deserts of southern Peru.
entries.content:
Peru

13 killed in tourist plane crash in Peru

August 1, 2026

The plane was taking tourists to see the Nazca Lines, a group of geoglyphs etched into the deserts of southern Peru.

A small plane carrying tourists to see Peru's famed Nazca Lines archaeological site crashed, killing all 13 people on board, authorities in Nazca province said on Saturday.

"We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died," said Police Major Jorge Andrade at the crash site in southern Peru.

Andrade also said that "given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors," adding that four bodies have been recovered so far.

Peru's local news site RPP reported that seven Italians, two Germans and two Spaniards were killed in the accident. There's no official confirmation about the nationalities of those aboard the plane.

The plane crashed shortly after 1:00 p.m. local time (1800 GMT) after taking off from the airport in the city of Pisco, located about 240 kilometers (150 miles) south of the capital, Lima.

What else do we know about the crash in the Peruvian desert?

​RPP reported that the small plane lost contact with the control tower minutes after takeoff.

The crash occurred in the area of Pueblo Viejo, about six kilometers from the city of Nazca and ​around 12 kilometers from the Nazca Lines site, according to local authorities.

Nazca's government said the plane was operated by local Peruvian company Aerodiana.

The airline was not immediately available for comment. However, on its website, Aerodiana says it has operated scenic flights over the Nazca lines for the last 14 years.

The reasons behind the plane crash are still unknown. Peruvian authorities said the incident is under investigation.

Tourist planes over Nazca Lines have crashed before too

Stretching across the desert near the city of Nazca, the Nazca Lines are a vast collection of geoglyphs created hundreds of years ago by Peru's Indigenous inhabitants. 

The famous desert geoglyphs, many depicting animals, can only be fully appreciated from the air or elevated viewing platforms.

The latest incident is not the first plane to crash near the site in recent decades.

In 2022, a plane crash killed seven people on board, including two Chileans and three Dutch nationals.

In 2010, another fatal crash killed four British tourists and two Peruvian crew members.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: How does eastern Europe commemorate the Roma Holocaust?
entries.summary: In 2015, the EU designated August 2 as the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany, the day is marked with memorial services, educational activites and public addresses. And in eastern Europe?
entries.content:
August 1, 2026

In 2015, the EU designated August 2 as the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany, the day is marked with memorial services, educational activites and public addresses. And in eastern Europe?

It took decades before Germany recognized the Romani Holocaust — the Nazi genocide of 500,000 European Roma and Sinti during World War II. Several more decades passed before the European Holocaust Memorial Day for Sinti and Roma became an official German and European day of remembrance, celebrated each year on August 2.

Based on initiatives by Polish Roma groups, the Nazi liquidation of the so-called "Gypsy Family Camp" in the Auschwitz-Birkenau Concentration and Extermination Camp on the evening of August 2-3, 1944, was first commemorated half a century later, in 1994. 

Thousands of deported Roma and Sinti had already been killed as a result of malnutrition and disease. That evening, thousands more were forced into gas chambers, shot and beaten to death by Nazi henchmen.

In 2015, the European Parliament declared this date the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany and other European countries, the genocide is commemorated by officials with the participation of government representatives. In some cases, representatives of European governments travel to the memorial site in Auschwitz.

In most cases, however, countries hold their own memorial services — particularly in central and southeastern Europe, where Nazi extermination commonly targeted Romani peoples. These days, such memorial days also take the opportunity to raise awareness for ongoing Antiziganism and the consequences it has. 

Poland: 15 years of commemoration

Poland, home to an estimated 30,000 Roma, has been observing August 2 since 2011. The ceremony routinely includes a visit by parliamentary and governmental representatives to the Auschwitz Memorial.

Another important day of remembrance is observed each year in the village of Szczurowa, east of Krakow, on July 3. It honors the memory of Polish Roma massacred by German troops in 1943. In 1956, Szczurowa became the first site of a European memorial for victims of the Romani Holocaust.

Other small towns and villages across southeastern Poland also commemorate the killing of Polish Roma during Nazi German occupation.

Czechia: A former pig farm turned memorial site

In the Czech Republic, where nearly 250,000 Roma live, August 2 has been an official day of remembrance since 2015. The most important ceremony is held in Lety, south of Prague, where Roma organizations have been commemorating the genocide for decades. This is the site where German Nazis established a concentration camp in 1940, and began deporting and imprisoning Romani families from occupied Bohemia from 1942 onward.

After the war, the site was used as a pig farm. It was closed in 2018, following a long controversy, and transformed into a place of remembrance.

Czech President Petr Pavel and then-Prime Minister Petr Fiala both attended the opening ceremony in April 2024.

Another memorial site is located in Hodonin north of Brno, at the location of a further Nazi concentration camp which imprisoned Romani people from Bohemia and Moravia. Here, one of the atrocities commemorated includes the mass deportation of Roma and Sinti to Auschwitz on August 21, 1943. 

Slovakia: Memorial Day established in 2005

Around half a million Roma live in Slovakia. Here, the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day has been observed on August 2 since 2005. The main ceremony is held at the Slovak National Uprising (SNU) museum in Banska Bystrica in central Slovakia. 

The museum honors the 1944 armed uprising against Nazi occupation. It was one of the largest anti-fascist movements in Europe during World War II.

The memorial ceremony is organized by the government's Plenipotentiary for Romani Communities and non-governmental Roma initiatives. Other representatives of the state or the presidential office also take part.

Hungary: Antiziganism yesterday and today

Around 600,000 Roma call Hungary home. Here, since 2005, various sites have been observing the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day on August 2, following a parliamentary resolution. In Budapest alone, there are three places of remembering for the Roma murdered during the Holocaust where commemorative events are held. The reason for these and numerous other memorial sites is that Hungarian Roma were the target of deportations and killings particularly following German occupation in 1944 and under the rule of the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist regime.

Historical remembrance in Hungary is also deeply intertwined with the racist murdering spree directed at Roma people between 2008 and 2009. In this time, four Hungarian neo-Nazis killed a total of six people and injured 55 others, some of them severely. They planned their final hate crime for the night of August 2, in the eastern village of Kisleta. 

Romania: Deportation to Transnistria

Romania, where around 2 million Roma live, Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed since 2020. The main event is held at the Holocaust Memorial in Bucharest, which was inaugurated in 2009. Under the dictator Ion Antonescu, who was allied with Nazi Germany, Romania independently organized the mass deportation of Jews and Roma to Transnistria, where about 380,000 Jews and 11,000 Roma were murdered in camps or died from hunger and disease. In 2025, President Nicusor Dan became the first Romanian head of state to personally attend the memorial service. 

In 2004, Romania designated October 9 as its official Holocaust Remembrance Day. It was on that day that Jewish citizens were first deported from the Bukovina region to Transnistria. The day also explicitly honors the memory of Roma who were deported and murdered by Antonescu's regime.

Bulgaria: Commemoration without day of remembrance

About 700,000 Roma call Bulgaria home. Here, August 2 has yet to be declared an official day of remembrance, but it is still marked with commemorative events organized by Roma organizations. Government and state representatives also take the occasion to issue commemorative statements. Although Bulgaria was allied with Nazi Germany, it resisted German demands to deport Jews and Roma. But groups were discriminated against through a wide range of racist laws, and effectively made second-class citizens.

Croatia: Focus on escape attempt

Croatia has a population of about 25,000 Roma. Its parliament only declared August 2 a day of remembrance in 2014. The main commemorative ceremony is held at the site of the former concentration and extermination camp Jasenovac, where the fascist Ustashe movement imprisoned Serbs, Jews, Croats and Roma.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 were murdered there. High-ranking politicians regularly take part in commemorative ceremonies. More broadly, remembrance events in Jasenovac primarily highlight April 22, when prisoners attempted to escape the extermination camp in 1945.

North Macedonia: Memorial Day and national holiday

Around 100,000 Roma live in North Macedonia, where the Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed on August 2 since 2017. A key remembrance ceremony is held in Skopje at the Holocaust Memorial Center for the Jews of Macedonia. In North Macedonia is also a national and religious holiday: Republic Day and St Elijah Day, respectively. because of this, public remembrance of the Roma genocide tends to receive less attention.

Serbia: No official day of remembrance

In Serbia, home to around 130,000 Roma, August 2 is not an official memorial day for the Roma genocide. But there are other days of remembering the genocidal policies of the Nazi and Ustase regimes which also honor the memory of the Roma killed in the genocide.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Germany news: Big turnout for Pride after Berlin attack
entries.summary: Several German cities are holding Pride events a week after a deadly attack on a march in Berlin. A forest fire is burning out of control in Bavaria. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Big turnout for Pride after Berlin attack

Published August 1, 2026last updated August 2, 2026

Several German cities are holding Pride events a week after a deadly attack on a march in Berlin. A forest fire is burning out of control in Bavaria. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Pride events are taking place in several German cities a week after a deadly attack on a Pride march in Berlin
  • Authorities warn of holiday traffic disruption in Germany amid the two-hour closure of a key pass road in Austria
  • A forest fire is burning out of control in the Upper Palatinate region of Bavaria, with four firefighters so far injured in the blaze

Here is a round-up of some of the main stories from and about Germany hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 1-2.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section We've paused coverage

We've paused coverage

Thank you for reading the weekend edition of our blog about Germany and be sure to check in on Sunday morning to stay up to date with the latest headlines out of the country.

Skip next section WATCH — Hamburg Pride draws 300,000 after Berlin terror attack

WATCH — Hamburg Pride draws 300,000 after Berlin terror attack

Hamburg's Pride parade went ahead under heightened security, one week after a 21-year-old drove a van into crowds at Berlin Pride. The attack killed one person and injured 29 others.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

IN DEPTH: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. 

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests: 260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

Read more about Germany's policy on deportations to Afghanistan.

Skip next section Klingbeil urges for solidarity with Spain over Ceuta border breach

Klingbeil urges for solidarity with Spain over Ceuta border breach

German Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil on Saturday called on Europeans to stand by Spain amid the debate over the surge of migrants into Ceuta.

Footage showing tens of thousands of migrants crossing into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta raised concerns across the European Union.

"Migrants were used in an attempt to divide Europe," Klingbeil said.

He noted that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had restored control quickly and that most migrants who entered Ceuta had already returned to Morocco.

"Especially in situations like these, Europe must not allow itself to be divided," Klingbeil said.

Klingbeil's comments come after Italy officially suspended the Schengen agreement with Spain for one month in response to the mass crossing in Ceuta.

Skip next section Popular German national park closed after storm leaves 1 dead

Popular German national park closed after storm leaves 1 dead

A popular park in eastern Germany was closed to visitors on Saturday after a storm caused damage and left one person dead overnight.

A 38-year-old man was killed on Friday evening near the Felsenbühne open-air theater in Rathen when he was struck by a falling tree.

Ten other people were injured, three of them seriously, while 40 people were evacuated.

Emergency crews resumed clean-up operations on Saturday.

Authorities closed the area between the Bastei rock formation, the villages of Rathen and Hohnstein, and the Polenztal valley, citing ongoing safety risks for visitors.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany weighs the future of minijobs

IN DEPTH: Germany weighs the future of minijobs

When Anahita Abdollahi starts her shift, she first checks her emails to make sure she's up to date on all the library requests.

The 26-year-old master's student from Iran describes her job as a "part-time librarian" — she helps people find books they need for their studies, answers phone calls, and waters the plants.

This type of employment is known in Germany as a "minijob," a system that allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions.

Skip next section WATCH: German development aid: Is soft power in decline?

WATCH: German development aid: Is soft power in decline?

German funding for projects abroad is falling. So is public support.

Nearly 8 in ten Germans say they are proud of supporting poorer countries. But only around 2 in ten say they understand what German development aid is actually trying to achieve.

In Argentina, young musicians show what that money can achieve. 

Skip next section Hamburg Pride returns with increased security a week after Berlin attack

Hamburg Pride returns with increased security a week after Berlin attack

Hundreds of thousands of people on Saturday gathered in the northern German port city of Hamburg for its annual Pride parade, one of Germany's biggest, one week after a deadly Islamist terrorist attack on Berlin Pride.

Among dozens of trucks marching through the center of Germany's second-biggest city was one representing Berlin's Pride event — known in Germany as Christopher Street Day or CSD for short.

Participants on the truck were asked to wear dark clothing in tribute to the victims of last week's attack.

"After the brutal attack on the CSD in Berlin, many are unsure in the queer community but also in society whether here and today is the right place," Hamburg's deputy mayor, Katharina Fegebank, told RTL television. "I say, now more than ever."

Both police and march organizers said the turnout was about 300,000 people.

Pride events also took place in Bonn and other cities across Germany.

Skip next section Rhine River hits record low in North Rhine-Westphalia

Rhine River hits record low in North Rhine-Westphalia

The river Rhine, one of the most important waterways in Germany, reached a historic low in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia on Saturday, authorities said.

Just 68 cm (26.77 inches) were measured at the gauge point in the city of Cologne, one centimeter below the previous record low of October 23, 2018.

The mean level at the gauge point ranges from 297 cm to 348 cm.

Gauge readings do not give the river's actual depth but rather the height of water above a given baseline. The shipping industry uses them to calculate what weights vessels using the waterway can carry.

The sinking water level comes as Germany, along with other parts of Europe, experiences low rainfall coupled with bouts of high summer temperatures that scientists say are a result of human-induced climate change.

The Rhine ⁠is an important ​route for commercial shipping and is used to transport commodities such as grains, minerals, ores, coal and oil products.

 A drought in 2022 that reduced water levels in the river caused supply bottlenecks and production problems affecting several companies.

Skip next section Forest fire breaks out in Bavaria

Forest fire breaks out in Bavaria

Some 330 emergency personnel have been deployed to fight a forest fire that broke out on Friday near Freudenberg in the Upper Palatinate region of Bavaria.

The fire is burning out of control in difficult terrain amid strong winds, local authorities said, with a thunderstorm hampering firefighting operations.

Four firefighters have been injured while battling the flames, local authorities said on Saturday.

People have been warned to avoid the area, while authorities have advised residents to keep windows and doors closed, turn off air conditioning and ventilation systems and follow local radio for further information.

Europe as a whole has seen several major blazes so far this seasonas human-induced climate change increasingly produces conditions conducive to their ignition.

Skip next section Train punctuality still 'not good' in first half of 2026 — DB head

Train punctuality still 'not good' in first half of 2026 — DB head

Just 58.7% of Germany's long-distance trains arrived on time at their destination in the first half of the year, with the head of national rail operator Deutsche Bahn (DB) conceding that there was much room for improvement.

"That is not a good figure. There's no point trying to gloss over it," Evelyn Palla told the Sunday edition of the Welt newspaper.

However, Palla, who took over as head of DB in October 2025, said the delay was less than 15 minutes in three-quarters of the cases.

"Even though we are not yet satisfied overall, we should not make Deutsche Bahn out to be worse than it is," she said.

DB considers a long-distance train delayed if it arrives at least six minutes late, with canceled trains included in the company's operational punctuality statistics.

Palla had set a punctuality target of at least 60% for this year and has worked to streamline the company by cutting several management positions, among other things.

DB has also begun to overhaul key lines as it seeks to improve its services, which have long been the object of criticism from those who rely on them. 

Skip next section Storms leave 1 dead in Saxony, cause disruption in Hamburg

Storms leave 1 dead in Saxony, cause disruption in Hamburg

A severe storm has hit the Saxon Switzerland region in the eastern state of Saxony, with a 28-year-old man killed by a falling tree, police said on Friday.

A number of other people were also injured, some seriously, amid the bad weather, they said.

The fatality occurred near the Felsenbühne open-air theater in the town of Rathen on Friday evening.

A performance of the musical "Little Shop of Horrors" at the theater, one of the largest open-air theaters in Saxony, was cancelled.

Parts of the Saxon Switzerland national park was closed to visitors on Saturday, with authorities saying there was still a risk from falling trees.

Germany's national meteorological service, the DWD, had issued warnings about severe thunderstorms for large parts of Saxony, saying there could be possible lightning strikes, falling trees and flying debris.

Meanwhile, a severe storm also swept the northern port city of Hamburg on Friday evening, with the fire brigade responding to almost 100 call-outs.

Most were water-related incidents.

No injuries were reported amid the storm, which was reported to have particularly affected the southern and northern outskirts of the city.

Skip next section Traffic disruption expected as Austrian pass road blocked

Traffic disruption expected as Austrian pass road blocked

Austria's Fern Pass road is to be closed for some two hours on Saturday morning amid a demonstration, with authorities warning of delays to holiday traffic as vacations get underway in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

The road is a key north-south transit route linking Germany, Austria and Italy.

Protesters are demonstrating not only at the volume of traffic on the route but also against a planned tunnel intended to replace the most difficult section of the road.

They say the project will only attract more traffic.

The nearby Hahntennjoch Pass will also be temporarily closed amid the protest, which is expected to be attended by hundreds of people.

The Fern Pass, which reaches an elevation of 1,212 meters (almost 4,000 feet), carries more traffic than almost any other pass in the eastern Alps, second only to the Brenner Pass.

Skip next section Pride events planned in several German cities after attack

Pride events planned in several German cities after attack

Pride events in several German cities are expected to draw hundreds of thousands of people on Saturday.

The events are to take place just a week after a man rammed a car into the Berlin Pride march, killing a woman and injuring 31 other people.German authorities said they were treating the incident as an "Islamist terrorist attack." The suspect was later shot dead by German police as they tried to arrest him.

In Hamburg, where some 250,000 people are expected to gather, police have announced that they will deploy twice as many officers as last year to protect the event.

The march is expected to feature a float from the Berlin organizers on which participants will wear dark clothing in tribute to the victims.

Pride events are also planned in the cities of Bonn, Ahaus and Moers in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and another in the eastern city of Naumburg in Saxony-Anhalt.

In Germany, such events are called Christopher Street Day (CSD) in commemoration of events in New York in 1969 after police raided the Stonewall Inn bar on Christopher Street.

The raids triggered days of protests by gay, lesbian and transgender people that became the starting point for a worldwide rights movement.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn says guten Tag to all its readers as we get underway with our look-round at stories with a Germany slant on the first day of the month.

Topping the list are the planned Pride events scheduled to take place across the country amid heightened security after a deadly attack a week ago on a march in Berlin.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to turn out in support of the LGBTQ+ community and societal diversity.

The summer is also bringing its share of extreme weather events and fires to Germany, with severe storms in the north and east and a major blaze in a southern forest.

Join us here for these and other stories from Europe's biggest economy!

entries.title: Germany's long road to equality for same-sex couples
entries.summary: In 2001, same-sex couples in Germany were able to register a civil partnership for the first time. The Civil Partnership Act was a crucial step toward "marriage for all," which was introduced in 2017.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's long road to equality for same-sex couples

August 1, 2026

In 2001, same-sex couples in Germany were able to register a civil partnership for the first time. The Civil Partnership Act was a crucial step toward "marriage for all," which was introduced in 2017.

August 1, 2001, marked a turning point: with the Civil Partnership Act, same-sex couples in Germany gained a legal framework for the registration of their partnerships. However, another 16 years would pass before marriage itself became an option.

"The Civil Partnership Act was a milestone for the legal recognition of same-sex couples in Germany and laid the foundation for opening up marriage," Alexander Vogt of the national board of "Queere Vielfalt e.V." (Queer diversity) told DW.

"It introduced a legally secure partnership with rights similar to those of marriage — such as inheritance, maintenance, and residency rights — though it remained discriminatory in many areas – like adoption or tax law. Nevertheless, it gave us a foot in the door — a solid base from which further rights could be secured, usually by appealing to the Federal Constitutional Court."

Public opinion was ahead of the political establishment

The legislation was preceded by a fierce political debate. The opposition bloc of conservative parties, the Christian Democratic Union and the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), denounced it as an "unconstitutional attack on marriage and the family." Lawmakers from the ruling center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, described the law as "a long-overdue act of redress."

"There was strong conservative opposition, for instance from churches and civic groups," Alexander Vogt noted. "The debate reflected the classic culture war between traditional and progressive values."

Backed by the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens, the majority of Bundestag lawmakers voted in favor of the Civil Partnership Act in November 2000, despite opposition from the CDU/CSU and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP).

German public opinion was already a step ahead: A 1999 survey showed that 55% of respondents were already in favor of the Civil Partnership Act.

However, Germany was by no means a pioneer. Denmark was the first country in the world to introduce civil partnerships for same-sex couples, doing so as early as 1989. Norway, Sweden, and Iceland followed in the mid-1990s, with France following in 1999.

'We simply wanted equal treatment'

Twenty-five years ago, Reinhard Lüschow and his husband Heinz-Friedrich Harre — who has since passed away — became the first same-sex couple in Germany to tie the knot at a registry office under the new Civil Partnership Act. They had spent the preceding decade fighting for legal recognition as a couple.

As early as 1992, they had made a public statement by applying to register their marriage — in a coordinated move by 250 male and female same-sex couples across Germany. When their application was rejected, they took the case all the way to the Federal Constitutional Court. "We simply wanted to be treated equally," Lüschow recently told the Protestant Press Service (epd).

Although the court ruled at the time that marriage was a union between a man and a woman, it also mandated that the legislature ensure same-sex partnerships were not discriminated against. When the Bundestag implemented this requirement through the Civil Partnership Act, Lüschow and Harre reacted immediately.

Hard-won changes

The Civil Partnership Act regulates matters such as the use of surnames, mutual financial support, and inheritance rights. In the years that followed, the scope of civil partnerships was gradually expanded — first in 2004 to include stepchild adoption, and later to achieve tax equality following several rulings by the Federal Constitutional Court.

The Civil Partnership Act was merely the first step toward equality. The decisive step did not come until October 1, 2017, with legislation that introduced so-called "marriage for all."

This, too, was a hard-won victory. The conservative parties had come to power again in 2005. They blocked the legislation until Chancellor Angela Merkel authorized a vote free from party-line constraints, meaning lawmakers were to follow only their consciences; this is how the majority was secured in 2017. Angela Merkel and current Chancellor Friedrich Merz voted against the legislation.

Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile were the first same-sex couple to marry. Reflecting on the 2001 Civil Partnership Act, Mende later told DW: "It was a second-class partnership." Although there were few legal restrictions, the status lacked the standing of a conventional marriage.

Married partners enjoy more rights — for instance, regarding naming laws, child adoption, and the equalization of pension rights. Marriage also carries greater recognition internationally.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 108,000 couples had availed themselves of this new option by 2025. At the same time, approximately 24,000 registered civil partnerships remain in existence; these can be converted into marriages upon application.

'Marriage for all' does not amount to full equality

Differences remain between same-sex and opposite-sex couples. Alexander Vogt of the association Queere Vielfalt cites an example regarding the law of parentage: "If a child is born into a family with two mothers, the non-biological mother must first go through an adoption process to establish legal parenthood. This is not the case for heterosexual couples."

Reflecting on societal developments, Vogt observes: "Acceptance of same-sex marriage has clearly increased."

However, he adds: "We have become more visible in recent years, but not safer; violence and hate crimes — particularly against queer people — have risen sharply. The figures have increased tenfold since 2010! The attack in Berlin represents a tragic peak in this trend, one that has garnered significant public attention."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan
entries.summary: Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. Faridoon Tofan, who is currently in deportation detention, fears the same fate.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

August 1, 2026

Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. Faridoon Tofan, who is currently in deportation detention, fears the same fate.

Things would likely have turned out very differently had Faridoon Tofan not taken the bus to Italy. He had intended to go on a short trip to Rome. The 46-year-old — who had fled the Taliban to Germany just under four years ago and had since been working and learning the language — was detained during a border check in mid-April and taken directly to a deportation detention center in Munich.

The reason: Tofan did not have the legal right to leave Germany. His asylum application had been rejected; he held only a temporary residence permit, which does not protect against deportation. He could now be sent back to Kabul, even though he is neither a convicted criminal nor has he been classified as a security threat. His asylum application appeal was definitively rejected in July, and he is now to be deported.

Tofan's wife and six children are still living in Kabul. They were recently paid a visit by Taliban officials and say they've been living in constant fear ever since and the sons no longer dare attend school, Nina Alizadeh Marandi told DW. She is an asylum law expert at the human rights organization Amnesty International in Germany and in close contact with Tofan's lawyer.

The Taliban officials' interest in the Tofan family in Kabul came after Faridoon Tofan's meeting with Afghan consulate staff in Berlin. Both the embassy in the German capital and the Afghan Consulate General in Bonn are now under Taliban control — a state of affairs for which the German government has faced heavy criticism from the opposition and human rights organizations.

While the German government does not officially recognize the Taliban administration as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, it points to contacts maintained at a purely "technical level."

Deportation precedent

This week, another Afghan national with no criminal record was deported.

The flight — operated by Freebird Airlines using an Airbus A320-214 — departed Leipzig/Halle Airport in Eastern Germany at 1:43 a.m. on Tuesday, bound for Trabzon, Turkey, before continuing to Kabul, Afghanistan. The Afghan national with no criminal record was on the plane alongside 30 convicted offenders.

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests: 260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

Luca Müller, spokesperson for the anti-racism group, also referenced the deadly terror attack on the Pride event in Berlin over the weekend: "While Islamist violence targeting Berlin's Pride celebration is being condemned from all sides, the federal government is supporting the Islamist Taliban through its deals," Müller said.

By "deals," Müller is referring to accusations leveled by many human rights organizations and the political opposition that the German government is de facto legitimizing the Taliban regime in Afghanistan in order to facilitate more deportations.

Interior Minister justifies the tough approach

What critics view as a breach of fundamental taboo, others see as nothing more than the swift enforcement of existing law. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt again told journalists this week, that anyone who has gone through an asylum process resulting in a rejection is therefore required to leave the country and must expect deportation if they do not depart voluntarily. Dobrindt, who is a member of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), stated that the federal government is simply pursuing its goals in migration policy, driving forward this "shift in migration policy" with "control, a clear course, and a firm stance," Dobrindt added.

Improved security situation in Afghanistan?

Since the resumption of deportations to Afghanistan in 2024, Germany has returned more than 200 individuals. According to Amnesty International, at least one of them was killed following his arrival in Kabul.

However, the German government points to assessments by the UN migration agency (IOM), which considers the return of men to Afghanistan to be feasible again — in principle.

"The security situation in Afghanistan has improved significantly; that is simply an objective fact," Mihyung Park, the IOM's country chief in Kabul, told the media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland. Park added one caveat: "Under current circumstances, we would strongly advise women against returning to Afghanistan."

In general, however, UN agencies warn against involuntary returns, noting that the returnees heavily depend on support to settle again in their country of origin.

Amnesty International condemns the German government for increasingly toughening its deportation practices without regard for the catastrophic human rights situation in Afghanistan. Nina Alizadeh Marandi pointed out that the very day of this week's historical deportation happened to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the adoption of the Geneva Refugee Convention.

"Human rights standards must not be eroded simply because upholding them is politically inconvenient," Alizadeh Marandi said. "Amnesty calls on the federal government to refrain from further deportations and to monitor whether Afghans who have already been deported are able to live in Afghanistan without persecution or danger to life and limb," she added.

Opposition speaks of a 'dangerous wrong turn'

Germany's political opposition has also sharply criticized the first deportation of an Afghan national with no criminal record. "It is irresponsible that Alexander Dobrindt is now deporting people to Afghanistan who have done absolutely nothing wrong here," said Marcel Emmerich, the Green Party's parliamentary spokesperson on interior policy.

Emmerich said that Dobrindt's "dirty deal" regarding deportations strengthens the Taliban, "makes us vulnerable to blackmail, and undermines Germany's own security." He added that the federal government is taking a "dangerous wrong turn" with this Afghanistan policy.

Juliane Nagel, a lawmaker for the socialist Left Party in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony, called the flight "shameful" and demanded that Saxony's Leipzig/Halle Airport — which is largely state-owned — no longer be used for deportations to Afghanistan.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Famed climber Nirmal Purja among 10 killed in avalanche
entries.summary: A major search was launched after an avalanche struck the expedition high on Pakistan's Broad Peak. The confirmation ended hopes of a rescue and marked the loss of one of the world's best-known high-altitude climbers.
entries.content:
August 1, 2026

A major search was launched after an avalanche struck the expedition high on Pakistan's Broad Peak. The confirmation ended hopes of a rescue and marked the loss of one of the world's best-known high-altitude climbers.

Celebrated climber Nirmal Purja and nine other mountaineers have been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, his expedition company said on Saturday.

The confirmation came a day after rescuers located four bodies while searching for the 10-member expedition.

How did Purja and the other mountaineers die?

"It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak," Purja's company Elite Expeditions said in a social media post.

"We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive."

The climbers had been missing since Thursday, when an avalanche struck the expedition at around 6,600 meters (21,650 feet) on Broad Peak. The party is believed to have been swept away.

Two Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters joined the operation on Friday, while an experienced ground team was deployed to the area where the group was last believed to have been.

Pakistani security sources said four bodies had been located that day, although they had not yet been recovered.

At the time, rescuers were still searching for the remaining members of the group.

The deaths of all 10 climbers were confirmed on Saturday.

The expedition included Purja and five other Nepalese climbers, including several Sherpa guides, as well as mountaineers from four other countries.

They were Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi, Omani climber Nathira Ahmed, US climber Mallory Geis and China's Wang Zhong.

Who was Nirmal Purja?

Nirmal Purja, widely known as Nims Dai, was a British-Nepali mountaineer who became one of the best-known high-altitude climbers of his generation.

The 43-year-old served with Britain's Brigade of Gurkhas and later the elite Special Boat Service before leaving the military to become a full-time mountaineer and guide.

Purja shot to international fame in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains above 8,000 meters in just over six months, dramatically beating the previous record of nearly eight years.

His feat was chronicled in the 2021 Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible," which helped bring him a global following.

In 2021, Purja was also part of the 10-member Nepali team that completed the first winter ascent of K2, the world's second-highest mountain.

Before the latest ascent, Purja had posted his hopes for the expedition on X, asking the mountain for safe passage.

What is Broad Peak?

Broad Peak stands at just over 8,000 meters in Pakistan's Karakoram range, close to the border with China. It is the world's 12th-highest mountain and lies only a few kilometers from the better-known K2.

Originally designated K3 during the surveying of the Karakoram, its more modern name refers to its unusually wide summit ridge, which stretches for roughly 1.5 kilometers (just under a mile).

The region contains five of the world's 14 peaks above 8,000 meters and attracts climbers from across the globe, although avalanches and rapidly changing weather make expeditions particularly dangerous.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic, Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
entries.summary: In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'

August 1, 2026

In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

Observing recent heatwaves in Europe, one pattern has often been remarked on: More women appear to be dying than men. During Europe's then-record summer of 2022, a study found 56% more heat-related deaths among women than men, drawing on mortality data from 35 countries.

Germany, which has just logged its deadliest heat season since 2016, with close to 9,800 heat-related deaths by mid-July, according to the Robert Koch Institute, is seeing the same pattern again this year.

Are hormones making heatwaves more dangerous for women?

Some of the recent coverage has leaned on the hormonal reading that women's bodies simply aren't equipped for heat. They sweat less, carry more body fat, and progesterone nudges core temperature up. 

But scientists who study the effect of heat on the human body say that's largely incorrect. "Overall, studies usually show only slightly more vulnerability to heat in women compared to men," saidAlexandra Schneider, an environmental epidemiologist and deputy director of the Institute of Epidemiology at Helmholtz Munich. "It's not really a very strong signal."

The small differences that do exist are real: Women do have a lower sweat rate, less skin area relative to body size, and fat distribution that affects thermoregulation. Hormones play a role too, but unevenly across a lifetime.

Schneider points to one group in particular: Women past menopause, when cardiovascular risk climbs. Older women with existing heart disease, she says, are probably at the highest risk of all.

But even in those cases, she doesn't think biology is the main cause for the extra deaths during a heatwave. "The living conditions, the social environment where women live, makes probably even more of a risk than just the differences in hormone status."

A research gap, not a biological difference

Toby Mündel, a kinesiology professor at Brock University in Canada, who studies extreme human environments, says that the impact is "overstated," when asked whether there's a real biological basis for the claim that women are more likely to die in heatwaves.

The factors that most determine how a person copes with a heatwave, Mündel says, are age, body size, fitness and habitual activity, and not biological sex.

Sweating is one example. Even though women do sweat less, that doesn't make them more vulnerable, because they compensate in another way. "They send blood flow to the skin, vasodilation, much better than males do," Mündel says, meaning their blood vessels widen more efficiently, moving heat to the surface where it can escape.

Pregnancy, which many assume must be dangerous, is another example. "As a woman progresses through pregnancy, she actually becomes better at handling heat," Mündel says. He draws a clear line between physiology and circumstance: There are good reasons not to have pregnant women doing heavy outdoor labor in extreme heat. But their bodies aren't the reason.

Why does the data suggest otherwise?

Partly, Mündel's argument is based on what gets measured. Studies often count hospital and emergency admissions, and women are far more likely than men to seek medical help. "That is not a physiological thing," he says. "Are they actually struggling, or have they just sought help earlier?"

Underneath it all sits a research gap. "We have about a hundred times as much data and evidence on men. We have nearly zero on women," Mündel says. "It's like comparing cats and dogs."

Numbers from Germany point in the same direction. The Robert Koch Institute attributes the higher female death toll to the fact that women make up a larger share of the oldest age groups. Its estimates also break down deaths per 100,000 people, and by that measure, the picture flips.

In every older age band this summer, the male death rate is higher than the female one. In other words, more women are dying in heatwaves only because more very old women are alive.

The real risk is exposure for women, not biology

If the gap isn't physiological, where does it come from?

Laurie Parsons, a researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, studieshow heat stress moves through the global economy in construction, garment factories, farming, driving, street vending.

Across the board, he says, women spend 30% to 50% more of their working time above heat-stress thresholds than men. In construction, when comparing men and women doing the same job, the figure rises to around 50%.

The reasons, he says, are structural. Women often wear more clothing for the same job. Men are more confident asking for breaks. And where men's work is visibly strenuous, it's recognized as a heat risk and rewarded with rest. But women's work is steadier, less obviously punishing, and gets no such relief.

Parsons compares it to the difference between a plane crash and asbestos exposure: One is a sudden, visible catastrophe, the other a slow, constant harm that's easy to miss. "Male heat stress tends to be this taller risk, where you get relatively visible moments of physical distress that can be managed," he says. "Female heat stress is constantly there, but much less visible, because it doesn't have those same obvious peaks in the working day."

Then the shift ends, he says. Men rest, but women cook, clean and care for children.

Heat also cuts into pay. Parsons says workers under heat stress are around 30% less productive in the garment sector, which he says is the easiest to quantify.

In formal jobs, workers make up for it with longer hours during the hottest part of the day, feeding what he calls "a vicious cycle" of worsening health and falling output. The self-employed have no such buffer. For them, heat stress just means less income, which ripples the wider family over time.

For Parsons, the starting premise is flawed. "Heat stress is not an atmospheric condition," he says. "It is a social condition, which happens within particular atmospheric circumstances."

Edited by Ben Knight

entries.title: Iran warns neighbors against being US 'defensive shield'
entries.summary: Iran has warned regional states against helping the US as Washington weighs possible "very hard" new strikes. Meanwhile, the Tehran-backed Houthis claim to have diverted eight Saudi tankers from the Red Sea. DW has more.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran warns neighbors against being US 'defensive shield'

Published August 1, 2026last updated August 2, 2026

Iran has warned regional states against helping the US as Washington weighs possible "very hard" new strikes. Meanwhile, the Tehran-backed Houthis claim to have diverted eight Saudi tankers from the Red Sea. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Tehran said any country acting as a shield for the US could be drawn into the war
  • Donald Trump has threatened to hit Iran 'very hard,' with US reports pointing to possible strikes on energy infrastructure
  • The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claim to have diverted eight Saudi oil tankers around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope

Read below for all the latest headlines on the Iran war on the weekend of August 1-2.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section We've paused coverage

We've paused coverage

US President Donald Trump told reporters on Friday he expected US military action against Iran to continue for some time. He said the US will hit Iran "very hard" until they can't take it anymore.

Hours later on Saturday, Kuwait said it responded to a new round of drone attacks from Iran while a tanker was struck in the strategic waterway.

We'll have more on each of those major news angles when we return to this blog on Sunday.

Skip next section UN warns against ongoing destruction in southern Lebanon

UN warns against ongoing destruction in southern Lebanon

The United Nations on Saturday said it is deeply concerned by ongoing Israeli demolitions in southern Lebanon.

Under a ceasefire deal, Lebanon's army is expected to disarm Iran-backed Hezbollah, while Israeli forces withdraw from designated zones in the south before Lebanese troops deploy.

"The scale of the detonations and demolitions taking place in south Lebanon is deeply concerning, with a devastating impact on civilian infrastructure, cultural heritage, and the collective memory of communities," the office of the UN special coordinator for Lebanon said in a statement on X.

The statement comes a day after the Israeli military triggered explosions near Beaufort Castle in southern Lebanon, which was added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger last week.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army destroyed "terror tunnels in the Beaufort area" using around 700 tonnes of explosives.

"The escalating pattern of destruction must stop as diplomatic channels exist to resolve any outstanding issues," the UN said.

Skip next section Gaza authorities say three killed in Israeli attacks

Gaza authorities say three killed in Israeli attacks

Israeli airstrikes killed three people in the Gaza Strip on Saturday according to Palestinian civil defense and health authority sources.

Israel said it had targeted "terrorists" and dismantled five weapons storage facilities in Saturday operations.

The attacks came on the heels of a recent announcement by US President Donald Trump promising the Islamist militant group Hamas would disarm and Israel's army would withdraw from Gaza.

Hamas led the October 7, 2023, surprise attacks on Israel that sparked the war in Gaza.

According to sources in the enclave, two Palestinians were killed in drone strikes in Gaza City and another man was killed during a missile strike on a hospital camp in Deir al-Balah.

Footage of the camp showed a large crater and scattered medical equipment, medical supplies and boxes near tents and two warehouses.

Israel accused Hamas of establishing a weapons depot at the site, citing intelligence reports without making evidence public.

Hospital workers said the warehouses were used to store essential dialysis equipment and supplies and that many people in need of critical medical care had been sheltering in tents near the site. 

A ceasefire has been in place in Gaza since October 2025, but Israel has recently killed suspected members of Hamas and the Islamic Jihad militant group there.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not commented on Trump's ceasefire plan for Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and Hamas disarmament. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has called the deal unacceptable, demanding the continuation of Israeli military operations in Gaza.

Skip next section Israel claims to have killed several Hezbollah fighters

Israel claims to have killed several Hezbollah fighters

Israel's military on Saturday said its forces killed several Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon. A post on the military's official X account said that one of its combat officers was injured during the armed encounter and had been hospitalized.

The post pledged that the Israeli military would "continue to operate to remove any threat its forces and will not allow the Hezbollah terror organization to harm the citizens of the state of Israel."

The incident came despite a ceasefire being in place between Israel and the Iranian-backed militants. While Hezbollah has formally denounced the deal, the group has not claimed any attacks since theUS-sponsored framework agreement was signed by Israel and Lebanon and then put in place in late June.

The agreement remains fragile, with Hezbollah refusing to disarm and Israel refusing to leave southern Lebanon — both points outlined in the agreement.

Despite the relative decline in violence in southern Lebanon, Israel has continued to conduct airstrikes and carry out other military operations.

Lebanon has condemned Israel's operations, saying that its continued military operations make it impossible to fully deploy the Lebanese army as outlined in the deal.

Skip next section US urges citizens to prepare to leave Middle East

US urges citizens to prepare to leave Middle East

US embassies across the Middle East have urged US nationals to consider leaving the region or be ready to depart if the conflict escalates further.

"Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation," security alerts posted by US missions in Amman, Jerusalem and Baghdad said.

The warnings told citizens to check flight information, follow local safety instructions and prepare for cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruption.

Those in Jordan were advised to stay away from US military bases, which have recently come under Iranian missile attack.

In Israel, US citizens were urged to identify the nearest bomb shelter.

"The Iranian regime is unpredictable," the US Embassy in Jerusalem said, citing recent attacks across the region and an expansion to areas not previously targeted, including Egypt.

A drone struck a US-owned gas vessel moored at an Egyptian port on Wednesday, sparking a fire. Egyptian authorities are investigating and have not publicly blamed any group.

Skip next section New attacks hit Kuwait and Strait of Hormuz shipping

New attacks hit Kuwait and Strait of Hormuz shipping

Kuwait's military says it is responding to a fresh wave of Iranian drone attacks that struck several "vital facilities" in the country.

Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi said the targets included a government facility in northern Kuwait. No casualties were reported.

Separate incidents also hit commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said an unidentified projectile struck a tanker on Friday about 11 nautical miles (20 kilometers) northeast of Lima, Oman, damaging its engine room.

On Saturday, another tanker reported a large splash and an explosion nearby while sailing around 21 nautical miles northwest of Khasab.

No casualties were reported in either maritime incident.

Iran has repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its authorization during the conflict with the United States.

Skip next section Houthis claim Saudi oil shipments diverted

Houthis claim Saudi oil shipments diverted

Yemen's Houthi movement says eight Saudi oil tankers have been pushed off their usual routes as part of a newly declared blockade targeting the kingdom's energy exports.

According to the Iran-backed group, the ships will now have to make the much longer journey around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope to reach Asian markets.

Riyadh has not confirmed that any tankers were diverted.

The Houthis announced the blockade last week, framing it as retaliation for what they describe as years of Saudi pressure on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

The group controls much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, after seizing territory in 2014 and setting off a war that drew in a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognized government.

A major concern for global shipping is the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow passage between Yemen and the Horn of Africa that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Any serious disruption there would add to pressure on trade routes already affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis said they do not intend to levy transit charges on vessels using the strait.

Skip next section Iran warns regional states against helping US

Iran warns regional states against helping US

Iran's military has accused the United States of "escalating tensions" in the Middle East and warned regional neighbors against supporting Washington during the conflict.

"The United States is rapidly moving down the path of escalating tensions in the region," Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran's military central command, said in a statement broadcast on state television on Saturday.

"Any country serving as [a] defensive shield for criminal and aggressive America will be engulfed by the flames of war," he added.

The warning came after US President Donald Trump again threatened to hit Iran "very hard."

US media reported that Trump was considering renewed large-scale strikes as early as this weekend, potentially including attacks on energy infrastructure.

Iran and the United States resumed exchanges of fire this week after several days of relative calm, although no strikes were reported overnight from Friday into Saturday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the situation in Iran and wider Middle East.

After US President Donald Trump again threatened to hit Iran, the head of Iran's military central command accused Washington of "escalating tensions" in the region.

Elsewhere, Yemen's Houthi movement says it has forced eight Saudi oil tankers away from their usual routes as part of a new blockade targeting the kingdom's energy exports.

Stay tuned for more news and analysis. For our previous day coverage of the conflict and the wider Middle East on July 31, 2026, you can catch our blog here.
